AI Operating System SOP

Installing a client AI Operating System, from the readiness check to a system the owner runs on their own. Draft, pending Daunte's review.

← All SOPs

v0.9 DRAFT, 2026-10-27. Owner: Daunte (method, governance, AI quality gate). Drafted by Eli. Reviews: Eli (delivery experience) and Kenny (commercial handoff). A draft until Daunte signs off. Covers installing a client AI Operating System, sold on its own (AI Jumpstart) or inside another package. This is the runnable path. The detail lives in the AI Jumpstart Delivery Playbook (how we run the engagement) and the bpp-ai-onboarding skill (how we build the workspace). When this SOP and those disagree, they win, and this SOP gets fixed.

What it is, in one line: a set of folders and instruction files that turns the AI tool a business owner already pays for into an assistant that knows their business. Say it to clients this way: "Right now the AI works like a contractor you brief from scratch every session. After this, it works like an employee who already has your files and follows your process."

It has three layers. Always name them in this order:

  1. Instructions: where everything is, how they work, and the hard rules.
  2. Context files: their business knowledge, written where the AI can read it.
  3. Workflows: step-by-step recipes for the jobs they repeat.

The whole flow at a glance (Workflows tier)

Stage Who What happens Done when
0. Set up Project lead Handoff, folders, Monday board, readiness check booked Paid. The readiness check is on the calendar
1. Readiness check Project lead and the client Their computer, AI plan, and where their files live Everything passes. Nothing else gets booked until it does
2. Kickoff Project lead and builder, with the client A screen-share tour of their business. Baseline number, access, the first homework Baseline written down, access working, homework sent
3. File audit Builder Read their files twice and write down what the call got wrong Written audit
4. Plan backward Builder End state, one number, session order Plan sent to the client
5. Build Builder, then the AI quality gate Context files, memory, workflows, setup guide, checks Daunte has passed it
6. Session 1: Install Builder with the client Fix something broken, install, connect, acceptance test, backup Acceptance test passes
7. Session 2: First workflow Builder with the client Run workflow 1 on live work One real output from the system
8. Session 3: They run one Client, builder watching The owner builds workflow 2 alone The owner did it without help
9. Session 4: Handoff Project lead and builder Cheat sheet, weekly routine, next build, asks The owner confirms it works. Status: validated

Session 3 is the product. Everything before it is setup. If the owner never runs it themselves, the engagement failed, however good the output looked.

Setup tier: one 90-minute session for someone who has never really used AI. They leave with an account, a place for their files, and two or three real uses on their own work. Run stages 0 and 1 first. For clients new to AI, teach in this order:

  1. One familiar business problem.
  2. The prepared result.
  3. The tools they already use.
  4. The AI work assistant.
  5. The headquarters.
  6. Human approval.
  7. Measurable business value.

Daunte's walkthrough leader guide in BPP HQ is the session script.

Pilot tier: not delivered yet. No SOP until the first one runs.

Inside another package (like Operator): the AI workspace is a priced line item on the quote and its own item on the Monday board, never a free extra. Run every stage that the quote's scope covers, and never skip stages 0 to 2.

Who does what

Role Owns
Deal owner The quote, every invoice, payment follow-up, HubSpot within 24 hours.
Engagement lead (project lead) Runs each client session, sends recaps and weekly updates, chases homework, keeps Monday current.
Builder The file audit, the workspace, the install, the acceptance test. Today that's Daunte or Eli, with Claude or Codex.
AI quality gate Daunte. Signs off on every AI deliverable before the client sees it.
Reviewers Eli reviews the delivery experience. Kenny reviews the commercial handoff.

The rules

The shared delivery rules apply here too (Website Development SOP): no work before payment, approvals in writing, every meeting booked at kickoff, a recap the same day, a reply within 24 hours, a weekly update, invites instead of passwords, and out-of-scope asks priced as change orders. On top of those:

  1. Use the AI tool they already pay for. Never make them buy a second one. If they're on ChatGPT, set them up in Codex. A ChatGPT Project that can't open their folders is the last resort.
  2. Their files are the truth. Read the real documents before writing anything about their business. Never write "the records don't say" until you've opened every file that could. A number taken from a planning document (goals, a lender deck) has to be confirmed out loud by the owner.
  3. Set the expectation: streamline, not automate. It does most of the work, and a person reviews before anything reaches a customer.
  4. The assistant drafts and never sends. Nothing goes out, gets posted or gets spent without the owner's OK. That's written into their instructions.
  5. Ship one workflow and prove one number. Name the other good ideas out loud as follow-on work. Don't absorb them.
  6. Check every tool capability against the vendor's own documentation before telling the client. When a client corrects a product name, re-check every fact attached to it.
  7. Use the status words exactly: draft, installed, pending sign-off, validated, live. Use the narrowest one that's true.
  8. No passwords, account numbers or personal ID numbers in any file the AI reads. Clients with sensitive information (minors, health, legal) get confidentiality rules in their instructions.
  9. One homework item at a time, designed so the AI does the reading and the owner only confirms a short list.
  10. Say plainly what it can't do. If one of their hoped-for uses won't work in their tool, tell them before they find out alone.

What's included (Workflows tier)

Included:

  • The instruction files.
  • Context files written from their own documents.
  • A memory log.
  • Four to six workflows, always including a weekly review.
  • A written setup guide.
  • The acceptance test.
  • A cheat sheet.
  • A written recommendation for what to build next.

Not included unless it's on the quote:

  • Connecting their software through APIs or custom integrations.
  • Accounting setup (the QuickBooks service).
  • An owner dashboard (the client Hub).
  • Custom software.
  • Their AI subscription. They pay for that themselves.

Prices come from the pricing hub.

Stage 0: Set up

Trigger: the quote is signed and paid.

  1. Fill in the sales-to-delivery handoff (Admin/sales-to-delivery-handoff.md). It covers what was sold, what was promised out loud, the real decision-maker, and which AI tool and plan they use.
  2. Set up the client folders. With Claude, run /bpp-onboard. By hand, follow the Website Development SOP, stage 0. Before the access-request email goes out, change it to ask for invites, not logins.
  3. On Monday, rename the milestone slots: M1 File audit and plan · M2 Workspace built and passed by the quality gate · M3 First workflow live · M4 Owner ran one alone. Mark the dates provisional.
  4. Book the readiness check. Book nothing else yet.

Stage 1: Readiness check (short call or screen share)

Goal: never run a session on a computer or account that can't handle the system. A setup session on a machine with no room, or an expired AI subscription, turns into hours of unpaid work.

Check, and write down the answers:

  • The computer: Mac or Windows and its version, how much memory (RAM) it has, and how much free disk space. It needs room for their files plus the AI app.
  • The AI plan: which tool and which plan, active and paid. The plan must be able to open a folder. If the work needs connectors, like HubSpot, the plan must include them; some only come on business plans. Ask on the call, not by email.
  • Where their files live: Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, or only on the computer. Agree how BPP will get access. On Google Drive, they'll share one folder with BPP's Google address; the engagement lead has it. If the files live only on the computer, plan a backup at session 1.
  • Who runs it day to day. That person comes to every session. It can't be handed to someone who wasn't in the room.

Done when: everything passes. If anything fails, fix it first, then book the kickoff and the sessions.

Stage 2: Kickoff (book 60 minutes and expect it to run long)

Goal: see how the business really runs, and leave with a baseline number, working access, and the first homework.

First 10 minutes, before the tour:

  • The baseline: "If this works, what one number changes? How long does that job take you today?"
  • Who else: "Who else does this work or approves it?"

Then let them drive a screen-share tour of their files, tools and real process. Ask:

  • "When a customer pushes back, what do you point at?" Whatever that is becomes the quality bar for everything the AI produces.
  • "Show me the file you open when you're pricing a job." Not "how do you price?" Their spreadsheet usually holds the whole system.
  • "When a new one comes in, what happens first? Which do you trust when two places disagree?"
  • "Can you share two or three proposals or contracts you won?"

Before you hang up:

  • Name what they built. Their system is usually better than you expect. Say so before you suggest anything.
  • Access: if their files are spread across accounts, make one folder on the call, drag everything in, and share it once.
  • Book every session.

After (same day):

  • Client recap with two asks:
    • The priority homework. If they already use an AI tool, send the AI memory extraction guide: prompts that make their AI write down what it knows about them. The context build is blocked until it comes back, so say so.
    • The won proposals or contracts again. It's the item clients forget most.
  • Internal notes: keep them separate, in Admin/Meetings/, and never attach them to a client email.

Done when: the baseline is written down, access works, and the homework is sent.

Stage 3: File audit (builder, no client time)

Goal: know what their files actually say before writing anything. The call always undersells them.

  1. Read the whole file store and map it.
  2. Find the spreadsheets that already hold their pricing, clients and pipeline. Most context files can come from these, without an interview.
  3. Look for:
    • broken formulas, placeholder numbers and empty columns;
    • a second system running beside the official one (a spreadsheet next to the CRM);
    • files they downloaded, edited and never put back.
  4. Ask before you call something broken. Look for the file where they explain why they did it. "These five lines are all the same number. Is that on purpose?"
  5. Read twice. The second pass goes into the folders that look boring (goals, reference, admin). That's where owners write about their own business.
  6. Write the audit:
    • the corrections to what the call told you;
    • three diagrams: their files, today's process (manual steps in orange, broken in red), and the target;
    • which context files can now be written;
    • what's off-limits.

Done when: the audit is written and saved in Working Files/.

Stage 4: Plan backward (builder)

  1. Draw the end state. Describe what a working day looks like after we leave: what they'll do, not what we'll build.
  2. Name the one number that proves it, measured before and after.
  3. List what has to be true for that end state. Each item is a context file, a fix or a habit.
  4. Sort by what blocks what. That order is the session order.
  5. Fill sessions from the end: the last is handoff, and the one before is the owner working alone. Anything that doesn't fit was never in scope. Name it as follow-on work.

After: send the client the plan with the end-state picture: "This is where we're going, here's what has to be true, here's the order."

Stage 5: Build (builder, then the AI quality gate)

  1. Write the context files from their own documents. Give every number a source and a date. Where a fact is unknown, write that it's unknown and what would settle it.
  2. Seed the memory log with 10 to 20 entries of their real history, oldest first.
  3. Draft the workflows, four to six, chosen from the jobs they actually repeat. Always include a weekly review. Workflow 1 gets finished with them in session 2. Workflow 2 is the one they build in session 3.
  4. Write the setup guide for their tool and computer. It explains how to open the whole workspace folder, never a single file. It does the mindset work too: you're training an assistant, not organizing files.
  5. Run the checks in the builder appendix, including the fresh-eyes check.
  6. Daunte's quality gate passes it before the client sees anything.

Done when: Daunte has passed it and it's saved, ready to install.

Stage 6: Session 1, install

  1. Open by fixing something real, like the broken formula from the audit. It takes 20 minutes, needs no AI, and proves you read their files. You can't automate on top of a broken calculation.
  2. Teach what the folder is before what it does: "This folder is the system. Don't delete or move it, and here's its backup." If their files live only on the computer, set up the backup now.
  3. Install the workspace beside their files. Don't move their files.
  4. Connect their AI app to the folder together, on screen. App screens change, so don't leave them to do it alone.
  5. Put their own spreadsheets on screen and have them confirm and correct the context files.
  6. Run the acceptance test with them: start a new chat in their AI tool, opened on the whole folder, with no files attached by hand, and paste the test from START-HERE.md.

Done when: the acceptance test passes.

Stage 7: Session 2, the first workflow

  1. Finish workflow 1 together and run it on live work, not a sample.
  2. Compare the output with what they'd have written themselves. If it isn't better, fix the context or the workflow, not the test.

Done when: one real output came out of the system and the owner would use it.

Stage 8: Session 3, they run one

  1. The owner builds workflow 2. You watch and keep your hands off.
  2. When something goes wrong, teach the recovery routine:
    • fix it;
    • check the fix worked;
    • update the instruction or workflow that allowed it;
    • run it again;
    • log it;
    • say out loud what changed. A silent fix teaches nobody.

Done when: the owner has built and run a workflow without help.

Stage 9: Session 4, handoff and closeout

  1. Run the acceptance test once more.
  2. Hand over:
    • The cheat sheet, with the five habits:
      1. Hand it the mess.
      2. Tell it, don't format it.
      3. Fix the instructions, not the answer.
      4. Stop re-explaining your business.
      5. Say "track this."
    • The one-page "this folder is the product" note: what never to delete or move, and where the backup is.
    • The weekly review workflow, put on their calendar. It's what keeps the system from going stale.
    • The written recommendation for what to build next.
  3. Set honest expectations. From the setup guide:
    • Week one is slower than doing it yourself; you're teaching, not delegating yet.
    • By week three you stop giving it background.

    • By month three you just ask for things.

      Weeks one and two are where almost everyone quits. Saying so up front is most of the fix. 4. Make the asks: the survey, a Google review, a testimonial, a referral, and the next build. 5. Change the status to validated only after the owner confirms it works for them.

After:

  • The builder records the handoff (builder appendix).
  • Log the lessons: client facts go in the client's files; a lesson that applies to other clients goes in the skill's lessons log, and in the Delivery Playbook's engagement log.
  • Close Monday and HubSpot.

Done when: the owner has confirmed it works, the status reads validated, and the next build is named.

When things go sideways

What happens What to do
The readiness check fails Fix it first, then book. A session on a machine or plan that can't run it is wasted.
They don't do the homework Cut it to one item only they can do, have the AI do the reading, and say what's blocked until it's done.
They edit downloaded copies Name the pattern. A stale file is worse than a missing one, because the AI trusts it.
We told them something wrong about a tool Correct it in writing, early: "One correction to what I said on the call." Then re-check every fact attached to it.
The work keeps growing Ship the one workflow first. Write the rest down as follow-on work, and price it later.
They can only use a tool that can't open folders Use the fallback: paste a short version of the rules into the tool, upload only the files it needs, and record the upload date and where the master copy lives. Tell them uploads go stale after any change.
The owner hands a session to someone else Reschedule. The person who'll run it has to be in the room.
They delete or move the folder Restore it from the backup, then walk through the one-page note again.

Words you'll hear

  • AI Operating System (AI OS): the folders, instructions, context files and workflows that make an AI tool work like a trained assistant.
  • AGENTS.md: the main instruction file. Codex reads it directly. Claude reads it through a three-line CLAUDE.md that points to it. A ChatGPT Project needs the rules pasted in.
  • Context file: one file of business facts, like pricing or clients, with where each fact came from.
  • Workflow: a recipe for a repeated job: when to use it, the prompt to paste, and what good output looks like.
  • Acceptance test: a fixed set of questions that proves the AI can find and use everything without help.
  • Baseline: the before-number we use to prove it worked.
  • New chat (fresh session): a brand-new conversation in their AI tool, opened on the whole folder, with nothing pasted or attached by hand.

Builder appendix (Daunte, Eli, Claude, Codex, future builders)

Workspace shape (full detail and templates are in the bpp-ai-onboarding skill):

``` / AGENTS.md short router: start here START-HERE.md human instructions and the read-only test PROJECT-STATUS.md where we are, what's next, file map CLAUDE.md Claude only: points to AGENTS.md

  1. AI Operating System/_system/ AGENTS.md the detailed operating contract _context/ one file per business area _memory/ current state plus a dated log _workflows/ 4-6 recipes, including the weekly review _setup/ folder map, access register, checklists _reference/ source register, decisions, approved examples ```

The detailed _system/AGENTS.md covers:

  • who they are;
  • a "current as of" date;
  • the context file table;
  • the precedence rule: the primary document beats memory, memory beats the context summary, and any conflict is raised out loud;
  • how to answer and how to write;
  • the memory format;
  • draft, never send;
  • what not to assume about this business;
  • the self-improvement loop (fix, verify, update, rerun, log, say what changed);
  • checking the workflows before any multi-step job;
  • when to route a question back to BPP.

Workflow format: one plain file per workflow, in three parts: When to use this, The prompt, and What good looks like. No tool-specific syntax.

Install without disrupting them

  1. Inventory their current structure.
  2. Back it up or preserve it.
  3. Add the root files and the AI OS folder beside their files.
  4. Map their folders.
  5. Update every path.
  6. Mark the system pending sign-off.
  7. If storage syncs selectively, make the root and the AI OS files available offline.

Connect a system only when its proof test passes. For each one, record:

  • what it's the authority for;
  • the account;
  • who approved it;
  • read or write access;
  • how access gets revoked;
  • one read-only proof test.

Acceptance test. In a fresh session on the full root, the test in START-HERE.md must name:

  1. the current milestone;
  2. where context, memory and workflows live;
  3. which source is the authority for what;
  4. what needs approval;
  5. the business folders;
  6. one known fact with its source;
  7. one open question it refuses to guess.

It doesn't count if any file was attached or pasted by hand. Record the result in PROJECT-STATUS.md.

Fresh-eyes check. Point an agent with no prior context at the folder. Ask three questions the files should answer and one they shouldn't. Verify every finding against the source documents before acting on it or dismissing it. If the test fails, fix the data, not the test.

Before delivery

  • No em dashes in any Markdown.
  • No empty files.
  • Every relative path resolves.
  • Build the zip with a Mac-safe tool.
  • If it's too big to email, send a share link.
  • If the workspace is local-only, the setup guide carries the backup warning.

Handoff record (in PROJECT-STATUS.md):

  • the master location;
  • the runtime;
  • the workflow that was tested, and the date;
  • open limitations;
  • the support route.

Status moves to validated only after the owner confirms it.

Where things go

  • Client-facing (recap, extraction guide, cheat sheet, next-build recommendation): Deliverables/.
  • Internal (meeting summaries, the file audit, the three diagrams, the automation opportunity map, the context plan): Admin/Meetings/ and Working Files/.
  • The best audit template so far is a client file-store inventory: a corrections table, the key systems one by one, the diagrams, a context-source table, and the off-limits paths. Ask Daunte for it.

Learning gate

  • A lesson from one client is a candidate in the skill's lessons log.
  • After a second client, or a controlled repeat test, it's proven.
  • It becomes standard once the skill, a template or a reference is updated and the evidence is named. Bump the skill version when a rule changes.
  • Add to the Delivery Playbook after every session.
  • Never create a second AI OS skill. Extend the one we have.
